name: Sourenee
tagline: A sardar's tea garden on the road up to Mirik
meta_description: Sourenee (Soureni) near Mirik: the 1902 tea estate, the Nepali sardar who first planted it, viewpoints over the Mechi valley and Nepal, and how to visit cheaply.
summary: Sourenee, also spelled Soureni, is a tea estate and village at about 1,330 m on the Siliguri–Mirik road, 7 km before Mirik. Its tea was first planted by the family of a Nepali sardar and formally established in 1902. Stop for the tea-slope views towards the Mechi valley and Nepal; shared jeeps to Mirik pass through.

local_story.title: Dakman Rai's land and the Tiwari brothers
paras: Most Darjeeling tea gardens were started by British planters. Sourenee's story begins differently. According to the estate's recorded history, a Nepali sardar, a labour contractor and headman, named Dakman Rai received land here from the British. His son Bhoujit began the first plantings of tea on the slopes. In 1902 the Tiwari brothers formally established the estate, and Sourenee has grown tea ever since.

The village that grew around the garden, recorded as Saurinibasti in the census, had 3,901 residents in 2011, most of them connected to tea. It sits on what is now the main road from Siliguri to Mirik, which turned a remote garden into a place every Mirik traveller passes. Look out of the window as you come through: the slopes fall away west towards the Mechi river, which marks the border with Nepal, and the bushes run in neat curves over the hills.

did_you_know: Sourenee's tea was formally established in 1902 by the Tiwari brothers, after first plantings by Bhoujit, son of the Nepali sardar Dakman Rai.
Saurinibasti, the village around the estate, had 3,901 residents at the 2011 census, with literacy of about 81 per cent.
Sourenee sits at about 1,330 m, roughly 165 m lower than Mirik town, and is about 7 km from the lake by road.
intro: Sourenee is the last tea garden you pass before Mirik on the road from Siliguri. For most people it is a view from a jeep window: endless curved rows of bushes, women plucking with baskets on their backs, and the hills of Nepal on the western horizon. It is worth more than that. Stop for an hour, walk a stretch of estate road, and look west across the Mechi valley.

There is no town here, just the estate, the village and a few roadside shops. Combine it with the Tingling viewpoint a little down the road and use Mirik, 7 km on, as your base. In the plucking season from March to November the slopes are busy and the light in the morning is soft and low. In winter they are pruned and quiet, but the views are clearest.

highlights.title: Tea slopes on the Mirik road
highlights.text: The road from Dudhia to Mirik runs straight through Sourenee's gardens, and the curved rows of bushes come right to the tarmac. Stop at a wide bend to look and photograph, well off the road.

highlights.title: View west to Nepal
highlights.text: From Sourenee the land falls towards the Mechi river, which marks the India–Nepal border, with the hills of eastern Nepal beyond. Best in the clear air of October to February.

highlights.title: A Nepali sardar's garden
highlights.text: Sourenee's history starts with a Nepali headman, Dakman Rai, and his son Bhoujit, before the Tiwari brothers formally established the estate in 1902. Ask in the village for the story as families tell it.

highlights.title: Walk to Mirik
highlights.text: Walk the 7 km road from Sourenee up to Mirik through tea and small villages, about 2–2.5 hours. Take a jeep for the bags.

highlights.title: Tingling next door
highlights.text: The Tingling viewpoint, over a bowl of tea gardens towards the Balason valley, is just down the road. See both in one stop.

how_to_reach.text: Every Siliguri–Mirik jeep passes through Sourenee; ask to be dropped, though you may pay the full fare to Mirik (₹150–200). From Mirik, local jeeps cost about ₹30–50.
On a car trip from Siliguri to Mirik, ask the driver to stop at Sourenee and Tingling; it adds 30–60 minutes. From Mirik, a car to Sourenee and Tingling and back costs about ₹700–1,000.
Walk from Mirik down the main road, about 7 km and 1.5–2 hours, or up from Sourenee to Mirik in 2–2.5 hours.

where_to_stay: Sourenee is best seen on the way to or from Mirik, 7 km away, where there are budget hotels in Krishnanagar from about ₹1,200 a double and the GTA's Swiss Cottages above the lake. There is also an upscale tea-garden resort on the estate road, outside our budget range. A few village homestays around Sourenee and Tingling take guests; ask in Mirik for current names, and expect about ₹1,200–1,800 per person with meals.
tips: Stop on wide bends or in lay-bys only; jeeps take these curves fast.
Come in the morning for the softest light on the slopes.
Clear days from October to February give the best view west to Nepal.
Do not walk between tea bushes or pick leaves.

experiences.title: Walk the Sourenee estate roads
experiences.summary: Leave the main road and walk the estate roads between the tea sections. In the plucking season, watch the leaf being picked and weighed; in winter, see the pruned bushes and the clear view west.
body: The main road gives you the view; the estate roads give you the garden. Walk down from the highway on a section road with someone from the village, between rows of bushes planted along the contours, past shade trees and small shrines.

In the plucking season, pluckers work along the rows with baskets on their backs. At set points in the day the leaf is weighed and recorded, then sent on to the factory. Ask before photographing, keep to the road and never walk between the bushes.
In winter the bushes are pruned and flat, and the work is mostly maintenance. The view to Nepal is at its clearest then.

faqs.q: Can I visit Sourenee tea estate?
faqs.a: You can walk public and estate roads and see the gardens from the main road. Factory visits depend on the estate's own rules and are not regular. Ask locally, and do not enter work areas without permission.

faqs.q: When is plucking season at Sourenee?
faqs.a: Roughly March to November, as in the rest of Darjeeling. First flush is in March and April, second flush in May and June, and autumn flush in October and November. The bushes are pruned and rest in winter.

faqs.q: Is Sourenee the same as Soureni?
faqs.a: Yes. The name is spelled Sourenee, Soureni or Saurini depending on the source; the census village is Saurinibasti. All refer to the tea estate and village 7 km before Mirik on the road from Siliguri.

experiences.title: The sardar who planted Sourenee
experiences.summary: Stop in the village and learn how Sourenee began: land given to a Nepali sardar, Dakman Rai, tea planted by his son Bhoujit, and the estate formally set up by the Tiwari brothers in 1902.
body: A sardar in the early Darjeeling tea industry was a headman and labour contractor who brought workers from eastern Nepal to the new gardens and supervised them. Some sardars became landholders in their own right. Sourenee's recorded history names one of them: Dakman Rai, who received land here from the British.

His son Bhoujit made the first plantings of tea. In 1902 the Tiwari brothers formally established the estate. The village around it, the descendants of the workers who came to plant and pluck, is still mainly a tea community.
Ask at a roadside tea stall or in the village whether anyone tells the family story. Versions differ; treat them as oral history alongside the written account.

faqs.q: What was a sardar in Darjeeling tea gardens?
faqs.a: A sardar was a headman and labour recruiter who brought workers, mostly from eastern Nepal, to the new tea gardens and supervised their work. Some became influential landholders. Their role was central to how the Darjeeling tea workforce formed in the nineteenth century.

faqs.q: When was Sourenee tea estate established?
faqs.a: The estate's recorded history says it was formally established in 1902 by the Tiwari brothers, after earlier plantings by Bhoujit, son of the Nepali sardar Dakman Rai, who had received the land from the British.

faqs.q: Who lives in Sourenee village today?
faqs.a: Mostly Nepali-speaking families, many descended from the workers who came to plant and pluck tea. The census village, Saurinibasti, had 3,901 residents in 2011. Tea remains the main work, along with small farming and shops on the Mirik road.

experiences.title: Looking west into Nepal
experiences.image_query: Mechi river valley Nepal border hills
experiences.summary: From the western edge of Sourenee's slopes, look down the Mechi valley to the India–Nepal border and the hills of Ilam district beyond. A quick stop with a big piece of geography.
body: The Mechi river rises in the hills west of Mirik and flows south to the plains, forming part of the border between India and Nepal. From Sourenee's western slopes you look down into its valley, with tea gardens on both sides of the border.

Across the river lie the hills of Ilam, eastern Nepal's own tea district. The tea grown there is very similar to Darjeeling's in climate and method; the border, not the hills, separates the two names.
Stop at a safe lay-by on the main road. Morning in the dry season gives the clearest view.

faqs.q: Can I see Nepal from Sourenee?
faqs.a: Yes. On clear days you look west across the Mechi valley into the hills of eastern Nepal, including the tea country of Ilam. The Mechi river forms part of the India–Nepal border here. October to February gives the clearest air.

faqs.q: Can I cross into Nepal from near Mirik?
faqs.a: Indian citizens can cross at recognised border points with valid ID; local people also use the crossing at Pashupatinagar above Mirik. Foreign nationals need a Nepal visa and should use a full immigration crossing such as Panitanki–Kakarbhitta near Siliguri. Rules change; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Ilam tea the same as Darjeeling tea?
faqs.a: Ilam, across the border in Nepal, grows tea in a similar climate and at similar heights, and much of it tastes alike. Only tea from the registered Darjeeling gardens can be sold as Darjeeling, a protected name since 2004.

experiences.title: Walk the 7 km road up to Mirik
experiences.summary: Get off the Siliguri jeep at Sourenee and walk the last 7 km to Mirik on the road through tea and villages. An easy climb of about 165 m, with the lake waiting at the end.
body: Most travellers ride straight into Mirik. Walking the last 7 km gives you time with the gardens: the plucking sections, small village shops, children walking to school and the curve of the hills opening as you climb.
The road climbs gently from about 1,330 m to Mirik's 1,495 m. Send your bags on with the jeep to your Mirik hotel if they will take them, or travel light.
Walk on the side facing traffic and take care on bends. Stop for tea in the village. Start in the morning to arrive in Mirik for lunch.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Sourenee to Mirik?
faqs.a: About 7 km by road with a gentle climb of roughly 165 m, which takes 2–2.5 hours at an easy pace with stops. It is a road walk, so traffic is the main hazard; keep to the edge and avoid walking after dark.

faqs.q: Can I send my bags ahead to Mirik?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Ask your jeep driver if he will drop your bag at your Mirik hotel for a small fee, or ask the hotel to send a car. Otherwise, travel with a light daypack and keep valuables with you.

faqs.q: Is the Sourenee to Mirik road busy?
faqs.a: Moderately. It is the main road from Siliguri, so jeeps, cars and trucks use it all day, heavier on weekends and holidays. Mornings on weekdays are quietest. Walk facing oncoming traffic.

faqs.q: Where is Sourenee?
faqs.a: Sourenee, also spelled Soureni, is a tea estate and village in the Mirik block of Darjeeling district, about 7 km before Mirik on the road from Siliguri via Dudhia. It sits at about 1,330 m, near the Tingling viewpoint.

faqs.q: Is Sourenee worth stopping at?
faqs.a: Yes, for 30 minutes to an hour on the way to Mirik. The tea slopes along the road are among the most photographed in the hills, and the view west to Nepal is wide. Combine it with Tingling, a short way down the road.

faqs.q: How do I get to Sourenee?
faqs.a: Any Siliguri–Mirik shared jeep passes through; ask to stop. A reserved car can stop on the way. From Mirik, a local jeep costs about ₹30–50, or a car to Sourenee and Tingling and back about ₹700–1,000.

faqs.q: Can I stay at Sourenee?
faqs.a: There is an upscale tea-garden resort on the estate, outside our budget range, and a few village homestays nearby. Most travellers stay in Mirik, 7 km away, where budget hotels start around ₹1,200 a double.

faqs.q: What is the history of Sourenee tea estate?
faqs.a: According to its recorded history, the Nepali sardar Dakman Rai received the land from the British, his son Bhoujit first planted tea, and the Tiwari brothers formally established the estate in 1902. It has produced tea since.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Sourenee?
faqs.a: March to May and October to November for green, busy gardens; October to February for the clearest views west to Nepal. The monsoon makes the slopes green but often hides the view in cloud.

faqs.q: Can I visit the tea factory at Sourenee?
faqs.a: Factory visits are not regular and depend on the estate's rules. You can walk the estate roads and watch plucking in season. Ask locally, and respect any 'no entry' signs at work areas.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Sourenee and Tingling?
faqs.a: They are neighbouring places on the same road. Sourenee is a tea estate and village with views west to Nepal; Tingling is the famous viewpoint over a bowl of tea gardens towards the Balason valley. Most travellers stop at both.

faqs.q: Is Sourenee safe for photography stops?
faqs.a: Yes, if you stop sensibly. Pull fully off the road at wide bends or lay-bys, never on blind curves, and watch for fast jeeps. Ask permission before photographing workers in the gardens.
